planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light, letting the cut ends callus a day before inserting; the reduced chlorophyll in variegated tissue makes this form slower to root and slower growing than the plain green species.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, lean, gritty succulent mix in bright indirect light, allowing the substrate to dry completely between waterings. This sport of string of pearls carries the same perfectly round, pea-sized, bead-like leaves, but each sphere is streaked and mottled with irregular patches of cream to white running alongside the translucent green stripe, giving the trailing strands a mottled, almost marbled look rather than the uniform green of the species. Because the white sectors carry no chlorophyll, this form grows more slowly and stays more compact than plain string of pearls, and it colors and holds its variegation best with several hours of bright light — low light causes the cream patches to fade back toward green. It is just as prone to stem and root rot from overwatering as the species, so err on the side of dry, and it carries the same toxicity to cats and dogs if ingested.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: String of Pickles (Ruby Necklace, Little Pickles)

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright light, letting the cut ends callus for a day or two before inserting; roots and new growth form quickly along the reddish stems.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun, watering only once the mix has dried completely. A South African trailing member of the daisy family (Asteraceae) rather than a true Senecio, it bears small, cylindrical, blue-green succulent leaves along thin, wine-red stems that trail or cascade a foot or more from a hanging basket or shelf edge; the leaves and stems flush deep ruby-purple under bright light and drought stress, giving the popular trade name Ruby Necklace. Cheerful small yellow daisy-like flowers appear on thin stalks above the foliage in winter and spring, a bloom display more prolific than most of its Senecio look-alikes. It is easily confused with string of bananas (Curio radicans) at a glance, but its leaves are shorter, more cylindrical than curved, and its red stem coloring and daisy flowers readily distinguish it up close; give it more sun than Senecio string-of types to keep the ruby color intense and the habit compact.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
